Vignette:
# Robert Chen: A Mugging That Wouldn't Release Him

Robert Chen had managed the Riverside Hotel downtown for twenty-three years without incident. At sixty-seven, he prided himself on knowing every corner of the property, every staff member's name, and the rhythms of the lobby at any hour. That changed on a Tuesday evening in March when he stayed late to review the next month's staffing schedule. At 9:15 p.m., walking to his car in the side lot, he was approached from behind by two men. One had been drinking—Robert remembered the smell of cheap whiskey mixed with something acrid, something that still caught in his nostrils at unexpected moments. The man grabbed his shoulder while the other demanded his wallet. Robert had resisted, a decision he had replayed a thousand times since. They threw him against the pavement, took his wallet and watch, and left him there with a split lip and a sense of violation so profound that it seemed to have rewired something fundamental in how he moved through the world.

The physical injuries healed within weeks. The rest did not. Within days of the mugging, Robert began scanning every person who entered the lobby with a different kind of attention—not the professional courtesy he had cultivated for two decades, but a calculus of threat. A guest in a wrinkled shirt, unshaven, moving with the loose-limbed gait of someone who had been drinking—Robert's chest would tighten. A delivery driver with an unfamiliar face, a contractor arriving early, a housekeeper's nephew visiting for the day—all of them registered as potential danger. His wife, Margaret, first noticed it when he began positioning himself at angles in their living room, his back never fully to a doorway. "You're always watching," she said one evening, not unkindly. "Watching for what?" He couldn't articulate it. The world, he had come to believe, was populated by people who would hurt you if given the chance. Trust was something he had surrendered the night his face met concrete.

By May, the hypervigilance had become exhausting. Robert would arrive at work an hour early, walking the perimeter of the building, checking the security cameras, speaking to the night staff about any unusual activity. His assistant manager, Derek, began to notice that Robert's mood had darkened, that he was scrutinizing staff in ways that felt excessive. When a longtime bellhop came to work with a cold and coughed near the front desk, Robert found himself thinking the man was unreliable, potentially unstable. The thought horrified him even as it took hold. He had become the kind of person who suspected everyone, and this realization only deepened his humiliation. He had been reduced to this—a man cowering in his own lobby, his own home, seeing predators in every shadow.

The startle responses had begun almost immediately. Margaret reached over to touch his arm one morning, and Robert jerked backward so violently he knocked over his coffee cup. At the hotel, when a staff member tapped his shoulder to ask a question, he would spin around with his hands raised, his heart hammering. He had apologized to Derek more times than he could count, each apology another small wound. He felt permanently marked by what had happened, as though everyone could see the fear written across him, and he found himself avoiding the staff break room where people gathered casually, laughed, touched each other in the easy way of colleagues who felt safe.

Even at home, behind locked doors with Margaret, Robert remained vigilant. He checked the locks twice before bed, positioned the bedroom furniture so he could see the doorway, and woke at the smallest sound—the house settling, a car passing outside, the refrigerator humming. Margaret had begun sleeping in the guest room. She had tried to be patient, but patience, Robert understood, had its limits.

He came to his first therapy appointment at sixty-seven years old, a man who had built a life of competence and control, now desperate to reclaim some version of the person he had been. What frightened him most was that the man he had been was gone, and what he feared most was that he might never trust anyone again.
